analysis.one_liner: Lets banks buy banks and open branches across state lines without needing each state's permission.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 1990 with no cosponsors, sent to a House Banking subcommittee, and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let bank holding companies acquire banks in other states even where state law forbids it, and let banks open branches in other states after 1993 unless a state had passed a law blocking it. It applied the same opening to savings-and-loan companies and foreign banks, and it let states that refused interstate branching be locked out of branching elsewhere. It never moved past its first committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Large multi-state bank holding companies, thrift holding companies, and foreign banks. They could buy banks in any state regardless of that state's laws and, after the end of 1993, open branches nationwide unless a state affirmatively outlawed it. Big out-of-state banks could also enter markets that had protected local institutions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large multi-state banks and foreign banks

how_it_helps.text: The Federal Reserve could approve a bank holding company's purchase of an out-of-state bank 'without regard to whether the laws of the State... permit or authorize the acquisition,' overriding state limits on out-of-state takeovers [S2][S3].

After December 31, 1993, insured banks, national banks, and foreign banks could branch into any state unless that state had enacted a statute prohibiting or limiting out-of-state branching, converting the default from state-by-state permission to nationwide branching with a state opt-out [S3].

Savings and loan holding companies got the same power to acquire thrifts across state lines regardless of state law, and states that refused to admit out-of-state banks would also be barred from branching into other states, a reciprocity penalty designed to pressure states into opening up [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Community and regional banks would face competition from national chains entering their markets, and state governments would lose their authority to decide which companies may buy or branch into banks chartered in their state. If consolidation followed, borrowers and depositors could face fewer locally owned banking choices.

drawbacks.text: The bill directly overrode state banking laws: acquisitions could be consummated 'notwithstanding any State law that would prohibit or otherwise limit such acquisition,' taking the decision away from the states [S2][S3].

Interstate acquisition and branching powers tend to concentrate banking in large companies; the bill contained no limits on size or market share beyond a temporary restriction on acquiring newly chartered banks before 1993 [S3].

The reciprocity provision punished states that kept branching restrictions by barring their own banks from branching elsewhere, a pressure tactic even for readers who support interstate banking on the merits [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have delivered real convenience gains for large banks and potentially simpler banking for customers, but its main effect was to strip states of their say over who buys their banks and to accelerate consolidation of the industry into large multi-state companies. Community banks and local control bore the cost. Coming just four years before Congress enacted a similar national framework, it reads as an early push by large-bank interests, and its design gave states little leverage.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to the House Banking Committee, then quietly passed to a subcommittee, where it died when the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Charles Schumer introduced the bill on July 26, 1990, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs [S1][S5].
On August 1, 1990, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions Supervision, Regulation and Insurance, and no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the House or Senate [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Community banks and state banking regulators, who kept state authority over out-of-state bank takeovers and branching for the time being. Large multi-state banks gained nothing from this bill, though the same policy was enacted nationally a few years later.

for.name: Rep. Charles Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Banking Committee; it was his only recorded action on it.

against.name: House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and never reported it out for a floor vote.

against.name: Subcommittee on Financial Institutions Supervision, Regulation and Insurance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on August 1, 1990, and took no action before the Congress ended.

against.name: Independent community banking groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed interstate banking and branching legislation of this era as a threat to locally owned banks.

sides.party_line_note: There were no roll-call votes and no cosponsors, so the bill never showed a partisan pattern of support or opposition; a Democrat from New York sponsored it and it drew no recorded allies.

industries.note: The bill let big out-of-state banks buy banks and open branches anywhere, overriding state gatekeeping. Customers could gain convenience, but consolidation into large chains could reduce local banking choices and local lending decisions.

Community banks would compete directly with national chains free to buy banks and branch into their markets regardless of state law, threatening the locally owned banking relationships many customers rely on.
Thrift holding companies got the same power to buy savings associations across state lines without state permission, expanding their reach at the expense of state authority.
Foreign banks could branch into other states under the same rules as domestic banks, while gaining Fed approval for out-of-state acquisitions.

industries.industry: State banking regulators and state governments
industries.note: States lost the power to decide which companies may acquire or branch into banks in their state, and states that refused to open up were barred from branching outward themselves.
